claims.text: A two-phase coexistence method can reliably predict the melting temperature of refractory materials.
A two-phase coexistence method can predict the entropy and enthalpy of fusion of refractory materials.
A two-phase coexistence method can predict the volume change at the melting point.
The proposed method has a lower computational cost than full thermodynamic integration.
The method can be implemented using either DFT molecular dynamics or DFT-guided machine-learning potentials.
A simulation cell containing crystalline solid and disordered liquid regions can be equilibrated under controlled pressure.
The solid-liquid interface mediates energy and structural exchange between the two phases.
At solid-liquid coexistence equilibrium, the simulated system naturally exhibits a temperature plateau.
Analysis of energy, volume, and entropy changes across the interface permits extraction of melting properties.
The temperature plateau corresponds to the melting transition.
The predicted melting properties will agree qualitatively and approximately quantitatively with experimental data.
The predicted melting properties will agree approximately with results from full free-energy integration.
Full thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamics is computationally intensive.
The simulation cell must be large enough to host a well-defined solid-liquid interface.
Machine-learning potentials used in the method must be accurately trained on DFT data.
Finite-size effects, machine-learning potential fitting errors, and DFT approximations can cause quantitative prediction errors.
Disagreement greater than approximately 10–15% relative to experiment or high-accuracy thermodynamic integration would falsify the claimed adequacy of the method.
